results.summary_before: This design is an interactive fixed-point Mandelbrot renderer that iterates z = z² + c in Q4.28 format and outputs the iteration count for each pixel. It uses a single sequential bit-serial shift-add multiplier shared across three products per iteration to reduce area. The host sends view packets containing the top-left corner, step size, and maximum iterations, and the chip outputs a pixel stream with valid, frame start, and line end strobes. It requires an RP2040 or similar microcontroller to bridge the parallel bus to USB for display, and a host viewer to compute view packets.

results.summary_before: This project is a bit-serial neural dataflow fabric with MAC cells on a self-routing banyan switch, accompanied by a 32-bit RISC-V core. The MAC cells are generated from a Lean model proved correct and then formally verified against their arithmetic specification. The design includes a 14-cycle frame protocol and supports edge input/output for streaming data. It is notable for its formal verification approach, though the sequencer and glue logic are not part of the proofs. No external hardware is required.

results.summary_before: This project implements the VLIW processor from the game HOVALAAG, a Zachlike assembly puzzle game. The processor uses 32-bit instructions and 12-bit I/O, which are shifted in and out serially over 10 clocks per processor clock. It can be tested by downloading the game's assembler to generate programs and feeding them through the serial interface. The design is notable for being a hardware implementation of a game CPU, created with permission from the game's author.

results.summary_before: This design implements a ring oscillator with skew correction using a differential clock ring. It includes grey counters to test the stability and frequency of the oscillator, with results displayed on a 7-segment display. The design is controlled by a select input to choose which counter to read, and it outputs a divided clock ratio. The original extended design did not fit in hardware, so only a subset is implemented.

results.summary_before: This project implements a small 4x4-bit memory using D flip-flops, where four data inputs are stored at an address selected by two address bits when write enable is asserted. The stored data is continuously output on four pins corresponding to the selected address. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and requires external clock, reset, write enable, address, and data switches, with outputs readable via LEDs. The design is a basic educational memory block with no silicon test results reported.
